opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I'm most excited about. SIMA has historically been trained and evaluated in a fixed set of commercial game environments and some research environments, and those are fantastic, but they're ultimately finite. Someone had to build each one, and once an agent has seen them, you're kind of limited in how much more it can learn from them.

What Genie 3 gives you is a way to generate an essentially unlimited stream of new worlds on demand. You can describe a scene with a text prompt, say a warehouse, a mountain trail, or a kitchen, and Genie 3 will produce an interactive environment that the agent can actually act in, in real time, with reasonable consistency over a few minutes. So instead of the agent adapting to the world we happened to build, we can start shaping the world around what the agent needs to learn.

In some of our early experiments we put SIMA into Genie 3 worlds and gave it goals like "walk to the red forklift" or "go find the packaging area." The interesting part is that neither model knows about the other's objective. Genie 3 is just simulating the consequences of the agent's actions, and SIMA is just trying to achieve its goal. Because Genie 3 has that world consistency, where things stay where they were when you look away and come back, the agent can actually pursue longer-horizon goals rather than everything dissolving into hallucination after a few seconds.

Longer term, I think this opens up something like an open-ended curriculum. You could imagine generating worlds that sit just at the edge of the agent's current capabilities, adding what we call promptable world events, changing the weather or introducing new objects or obstacles, to test robustness and counterfactuals. That's very hard to do with handcrafted environments. And that's really the bet for embodied agents: if we want generally capable agents, maybe eventually ones that transfer to the real world, they'll need far more diverse experience than we could ever build by hand.

There are still real limitations. The action space is fairly constrained, interactions are only coherent for a few minutes, and getting multiple agents interacting in the same world is still hard. But as a direction, I think world models like Genie could be to agent training what large internet datasets were to language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to frame it is that for a long time, the bottleneck for embodied agents like SIMA hasn't really been the learning algorithms, it's been the environments. SIMA was trained across a set of commercial video games and research environments, and that's a fantastic diversity of worlds, but it's still finite. Every game has a fixed set of mechanics, a fixed set of situations, and the agent eventually saturates on what it can experience there.

What Genie 3 gives you is a world model that can generate interactive 3D environments from a text prompt, in real time, with consistency over minutes rather than seconds. So suddenly the environment itself becomes something you can sample from. If you want the agent to practice navigating a cluttered warehouse, or a flooded street, or a forest at dusk, you just describe it. You don't need a game studio to have built that level, and you don't need to hand-engineer a simulator for it.

And I think there are a few things that are really exciting about that combination. The first is just scale and diversity. You can generate an essentially unbounded curriculum of worlds, and that matters because generalization is really about the breadth of what you've seen. The second is controllability. Genie 3 has these promptable world events, so you can inject things into the world while the agent is acting, like changing the weather or spawning a new object, which lets you test counterfactuals and build targeted scenarios for exactly the skills the agent is weak on. That's very hard to do in a traditional game.

The third, and maybe the one I'm most interested in from a research perspective, is that it starts to close the loop. You have a world model that proposes environments, an agent that acts in them, and then the agent's successes and failures can inform what worlds you generate next. That's the open-endedness story that a lot of us have been pushing on for years, where the environment and the agent co-evolve. Genie 3 is really the first time the environment generator is powerful enough that the loop feels genuinely viable at the scale of rich 3D worlds.

Now, I want to be honest about where we are. The worlds aren't perfect, the action space is still fairly limited compared to a real game, and we've only run early experiments putting SIMA inside Genie 3 worlds. But even in those early tests, you see the agent follow instructions like "go to the red truck" in a world that didn't exist five seconds ago, and that's a pretty striking demonstration that these two lines of work are converging. The longer-term vision is that the agent's experience is no longer capped by what humans have built, and that's a fundamentally different regime for training embodied AI.

r002.rationale: It describes SIMA following an instruction such as “go to the red truck” in a Genie 3 world that did not exist moments earlier, after noting SIMA’s training in existing games.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss withholding SIMA’s goal from Genie or the risk that Genie might make the goal happen because it knows the intended outcome.

r004.rationale: It says SIMA’s successes and failures can guide which worlds are generated next, but does not clearly state that action-dependent goal success is a basis for SIMA to learn from its experience.

r005.rationale: It mentions injecting events such as weather changes or new objects to test counterfactuals and target weak skills, but does not clearly propose training agents to be robust to unexpected disruptions.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that Genie 3 can expand the range of worlds an agent like SIMA gets to experience. Instead of being limited to a fixed set of environments, you can imagine generating new situations that challenge the agent in different ways—different layouts, different objects, different tasks.

That gives you a way to ask whether the agent has learned something transferable. Can it follow an instruction and adapt when the world is unfamiliar, rather than relying on patterns from an environment it has seen before?

And potentially, you can use what the agent struggles with to guide what you generate next. So the world model becomes a way to create a richer learning curriculum. The important question then is whether that broader experience translates into more robust behavior in other environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing is that Genie 3 could give agents like SIMA a much broader range of worlds to learn in. With a conventional game or simulator, you’re working within environments that people have built. With a world model, you can start generating new situations and letting an agent interact with them.

That creates an interesting possibility: you could ask for a world that challenges a particular capability, put the agent into it, and see how it responds. Can it follow instructions in an unfamiliar setting? Can it adapt when the layout or the objects change? The goal is to learn skills that carry across environments, rather than becoming very good at one particular game.

Of course, generating diverse worlds doesn’t automatically mean you get a more capable agent. You still need to establish that those worlds provide useful, consistent learning experiences and that the skills transfer. But it opens up a really exciting direction for expanding the experience available to these agents.
